All 10 Tampa 6 St. Petersburg 4 Temple Terrace 0 Safety Harbor 0 Dunedin 0 Pinellas Park 0 New Port Richey 0 Ybor City 0 New on the list 5 Family-friendly 6 Great for groups 7 Recently opened 0 50 Cybel 👥 Family-friendly 🎉 Great for groups Chef Taoufik Abdelmoula made a name for himself running a pop-up at St. Petersburg’s Foodie Labs, where he introduced Tampa Bay diners to the wonder that is the French taco. The design-your-own mashup inspired by a classic late-night Parisian snack featured tortillas wrapped up like a burrito and filled with crispy french fries, grilled meats, vegetables and sauce. Abdelmoula quickly garnered a cultlike following for the dish, and those fans followed him to Cybel, the Moroccan-born chef’s first brick-and-mortar restaurant. Since then, the chef has only expanded his repertoire, with a full menu of tasty French- and Moroccan-inspired specialties — along with a fast-casual line called Lilya’s Cafe, where grab-and-go snacks like flatbreads, salads and pastries have amassed their own following. The Un Peu de Tout (“a little bit of everything”) is still the best way to start a meal here, with emerald green tabbouleh and falafel sidling a trio of dips — labneh, hummus and baba ghanoush — all served with puffy rounds of za’atar pita bread. After that, look no further than the spot’s lamb tagine, cooked in the traditional conical ceramic vessels with savory hunks of fall-from-the-bone lamb paired with stewed apricots and almonds. Don’t skip: Un Peu de Tout, French taco, lamb tagine 49 Raices 🆕 New on the list 🎉 Great for groups If the crimson 1950s Chevrolet outside doesn’t catch your eye, the bright and colorful dishes at this modern Cuban restaurant certainly will. Raices, which opened last fall off Dale Mabry Highway, is one of the most vibrant new additions to Tampa’s dining scene. Yes, this is a place to turn it up over a few mojitos, with live music on the weekends on the outdoor patio. But the food, which features contemporary and creative takes on classic Cuban dishes, is also very good. Golden-fried tostones come topped with roasted pork, avocado and pickled red onions, a perfect combo of acid, fat and crunch. Dishes like the ropa vieja and excellent vaca frita pay homage to Cuba’s culinary traditions, with a few creative tweaks along the way (in the vaca frita, shredded, braised beef is fried until crispy, piled high with red onions and drizzled in crema and chimichurri). Fufu de platano, a Cuban comfort food of mashed plantains, arrives tucked beneath crispy, perfectly cooked hunks of pork belly. And even the most unassuming dishes — a simple roast chicken, say, or a bowl of frijoles negros (black beans) — manage to impress and delight. Don’t skip: vaca frita, fufu de platano, tostones preparados 48 86 Wine Bar 🆕 New on the list When Shane Schuch and Kendra Hardesty opened their wine bar and restaurant last fall, it appeared poised for great things. The sleek architecture and decor, vinyl vibes and ambitious wine program at 86 Wine Bar ushered in an exciting new chapter for a burgeoning strip of St. Petersburg’s Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Street corridor. Things came together piecemeal. An expanding wine list here, a pop-up or new menu there, before slowly and steadily the couple’s approach fell into focus. Now, a year later, the bar has become one of the ‘Burg’s best spots to grab a glass of wine and chill. The food has been in a constant state of evolution. That’s included a brilliant play on a Caesar salad made with savoy cabbage, pickled golden beets, snap peas and a generous shower of pecorino cheese, as well a delicious hamachi crudo that arrived swimming in a tom yum buttermilk with cilantro oil, corn nuts, cucumbers, Korean pears and pickled mushrooms. title: 'Leaders all over the world understand that Trump is only there for two more years & then he's gone'
source_excerpt: In American politics, the possession of presidential power does not necessarily guarantee the capacity to exercise it. Few contemporary leaders have embodied this contradiction as dramatically as Donald Trump. Following what political scientist Ian Bremmer describes as the most consequential electoral reversal for a governing party in more than half a century, the founder of Eurasia Group and GZERO Media argues that the United States has entered a new political phase: the beginning of the end of Trump's capacity to dominate the domestic and international agenda. In this wide-ranging interview with France 24, Bremmer revisits his provocative thesis that America has already reached "peak Trump." Far from suggesting that the president has become powerless, he contends that his authority is increasingly constrained by congressional opposition, Republican discontent, unpopular foreign policy decisions and the growing awareness among international leaders that the present administration has a limited political horizon. The historical reversal is, in Bremmer's account, extraordinary: "Trump back in 2024 engineered for himself the biggest political comeback in American political history. And now, only two years later, the biggest loss in 50 years." At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental distinction between institutional authority and political influence. Trump remains commander-in-chief, retains the instruments of executive government and continues to command extraordinary media attention. Yet Bremmer argues that the president's ability to translate those advantages into effective political outcomes is diminishing. The consequences, he suggests, extend far beyond Washington. From the war in Iran and the unresolved conflict in Ukraine to the future of transatlantic relations, America's allies and adversaries are beginning to adjust their strategic calculations to a post-Trump political landscape. As Bremmer puts it: "Those foreign leaders will start to engage more with the America that they expect to deal with after Trump is gone." Equally significant is his diagnosis of the domestic forces driving this transformation. Economic disillusionment, unfulfilled electoral promises and accusations of political self-interest have, in his assessment, undermined the very coalition that propelled Trump back to the White House. Meanwhile, the president's apparent preoccupation with monumental projects and personal legacy raises a deeper question about the relationship between political spectacle and the responsibilities of governance. Bremmer's conclusion is unambiguous: "Yes, two more years to go. But nowhere near the level of disruption that he had on the global stage at the beginning of this term." The interview ultimately raises a question of profound significance for American democracy and the international order: Can a president retain the formal powers of the world's most consequential political office while progressively losing the political authority necessary to shape its future? Bremmer believes that process is already underway.
